leads.why: The PoolManager holds 34.4 percent of the supply. The finding rests on the public repository for the body of the rebase functions, and the deployed version has a different signature. A second bytes32 argument suggests rebases that follow a message from another chain, and the party that can send that message decides whether the hazard stays with the issuer.

leads.question: What are Varlamore USDC Growth at 0x2ba39e5388ac6c702cb29aea78d52aa66832f1ee (2.06 billion units in the PoolManager, symbol USDC, 18 decimals, owner 0xd8454b3787c6aab1cf2846af7882f8c440c3903d), EverValueCoin at 0x45d9831d8751b2325f3dbf48db748723726e1c8c and VSN at 0x6fbbbd8bfb1cd3986b1d05e7861a0f62f87db74b, and do any of them change balances without a transfer or carry owner controls?
leads.why: The price list puts them at 4.37M, 0.98M and 0.54M USD in the Arbitrum One PoolManager and I did not confirm the prices or read the contracts. A token that copies the USDC symbol with a large pooled balance can mislead users of interfaces that show symbols.

leads.question: Does the restricted wallet 0x42607b2e4fde22e83822d4a86ddac58d847dc289, or any other listed account, hold claims or liquidity positions in the PoolManager 0x8366a39cc670b4001a1121b8f6a443a643e40951, and has it set an operator or an allowance for them?
leads.why: Claim transfers match none of the documented event rules and make no call to the holder. An operator approved before the listing could move such claims out through transferFrom or burn. If that happened, the chain operator's remedies are a new rule or an entry for the PoolManager address, and the second would fail every exit (F-001).

leads.question: Who signs the storage writes that 0xb7541f225385104347539397a4e01abc1d4ea8bd (implementation 0x1b5a16e81ab8154559ec2f457fa61062a6b8876f) executes on Dinari USD+ at 0xfc90518d5136585ba45e34ed5e1d108bd3950cfa, how do the signed messages reach the submitting account 0x4d0d668410c765cdee19c0ef2f0523fc231e879f, and does any other function of that contract make it call the token with caller chosen data?
leads.why: The token accepts selector 0x8078438b from that contract and the call names raw storage slots, so the holder of the signer account can set the index, a share balance or the restrictor address. Submission is open to any sender. An account that obtains an unused signed write raising the index can run it between its own sync and settle and be credited the rise on 1.07M pooled USD+ (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 358-364). The cleared item on USD+ did not know this route. Decompile the two implementations, find the digest and the replay guard, recover the signer from the two used signatures, and check whether signed messages are published anywhere before they land.

leads.question: The PoolManager holds 1,070,677.64 USD+ against a net inflow of 1,070,699.89 by Transfer logs. Is the 22.25 USD+ shortfall booked to the one position in pool 0x12d6df7390ed2fd24b259c0737dcaaf58116ca29cd96c758c5bf5a948fb28b8c (USDC/USD+, fee 0.3 percent, no hook, PositionManager token 127727 of 0xcd04ccbf1cd5d18c9735b59f5e41f03a2941ebad), and is that account tied to the party that moved the index?
leads.why: The index was raised to exactly 1.0707 two minutes before the deposit of exactly 1,000,000 shares and lowered 3.5 hours later, and the pool has offered USD+ at about 0.70 USDC since with almost no trades. If the liquidity provider and the signer are one party, the exposure of others is limited to swappers in that pool. If they are not, this is a recorded case of an issuer side balance cut inside the PoolManager and belongs with F-086 and F-087. A full removal of the position must take 22.25 USD+ more than the PoolManager holds, which meets the limit described in F-083.

leads.question: USDG on Arbitrum One is the Paxos claimable rewards build with payout groups. Which accounts hold PAYOUT_GROUP_REGISTRAR_ROLE and CLAIM_OPERATOR_ROLE, can the PoolManager address be put into a payout group without a call from it, and who then receives the rewards that accrue on the pooled 1.69M USDG?
leads.why: balanceOf excludes unclaimed rewards and a claim moves USDG from the claim source to a destination the claimer names (ClaimableRewardsBase.sol lines 314-378 and 429-457 in the Sourcify source of 0x031610e2d186d78d3defbf907f56d1eac843d9de). Today payoutGroupIdOf(PoolManager) is 0 and partner signed registrations are off, so nothing accrues. A registration would direct yield on pooled funds to a third party, and a claim with the PoolManager as destination between a sync and a settle would be credited to the settler. The facets that hold registration and claims were not read.

leads.question: On each network, is there a contract X other than a pooled token on which transfer(address,uint256), called by a holder, moves the holder balance of a pooled token T, while X.balanceOf reports a different ledger that an ordinary account can raise more cheaply than by paying T? Method: with a stub at the PoolManager address call X.transfer(sink, 1) and read balanceOf(PoolManager) of every pooled token before and after. Candidates: legacy and second entry point addresses of pooled tokens, retired proxies, migrator and bridge forwarders, and system contracts that move tokens without an allowance.
leads.why: The settlement layer credits one payment once however many ids measure the same balance, which the face tests of this unit showed again on Celo, Arc and Polygon. The one shape that would break custody through take, sync and settle is an id whose transfer moves a pooled token while its balanceOf measures something else. Earlier sweeps compared balanceOf values across tokens and read the ledger of X itself, and did not read the balances of other tokens around a call to X.

leads.question: After Jenner activates on BNB Smart Chain mainnet at 2026-12-08 02:30 UTC, repeat enshrined.py, inherited.py and deleg_token.py of this unit there: do never created CAS20 addresses revert on balanceOf, transfer and empty calldata as on Chapel, do created tokens reject DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE with the PoolManager as inherited caller, and does an account whose designator names a CAS20 token fail every call?
leads.why: Until the fork every address of the range is a codeless account, for which take succeeds and moves nothing. The after-state was read on the Chapel testnet and from the master branch, and mainnet may activate with another release.

leads.question: Does the Avalanche C-Chain accept set code transactions, and from which upgrade? The public endpoint (avalanchego 1.15.3) executed a 0xef0100 designator placed by state override as code and failed with invalid opcode 0xef, while the other 20 endpoints resolved it.
leads.why: Several recorded hazards need a delegated account (code that can change behind a hook or token address, an origin check that a delegation removes). If the C-Chain has no delegations these do not apply there, and if it adds them at a fork the tests of this unit should be repeated.

leads.question: Can native value reach the Arc PoolManager without a call to settle or settleFor, for example as the beneficiary of SELFDESTRUCT, as a fee or reward recipient, or through a system transfer, while 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 is the synced currency? Read the SELFDESTRUCT and transfer rules in crates/evm of arc-node and state the answer.
leads.why: balanceOf at 0x3600... is the native balance divided by 10^12 and rounded down (2448892234477 units against 2448892234477765867401833 wei at block 32,753,089). An inflow smaller than 10^12 wei that lifts the remainder over 10^12 between sync and settle is credited as one whole unit (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), which take then pays as 10^12 wei. The gain is below 0.000001 USDC per settle and is paid from the remainder that native payers left, so it is dust, and no other path to it exists because settle rejects value while a token is synced (356). The answer would close the last open detail of the native face item.

leads.question: Compile this checkout with solc 0.8.26 and the settings of foundry.toml on a machine that has the compiler, then run the three read-only probes in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-test-pins.work (probe.py, probe2.py, probe3.py) against the built runtime bytecode placed by state override at an unused address on each of the 21 RPC endpoints. Do the 16 words of probe3, the lock and reset words of probe2 and the guard words of probe match the answers recorded for the deployed contracts?
leads.why: Every behaviour test so far ran against the contracts deployed today, which are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. The repository's tests as the CI runs them would pass without the end check of unlock, without the lock close and without the reset of the synced currency. The probes test exactly those statements and need no comparison of code copies. The immutable address in NoDelegateCall must be set to the override address when the runtime code is prepared.

leads.question: Does any hook test under test/ move one delta slot from a nonzero value to another nonzero value and then complete the unlock or assert the count, so that the condition previous == 0 at src/PoolManager.sol:375 is pinned?
leads.why: This unit found no such case in the router and ActionsRouter tests and did not trace every hook test. An increment on every nonzero result would block callers that touch one currency twice, which is a freeze without a theft.

leads.question: Which Foundry version will the pre-deployment test run use, and does it isolate top level calls by default? On the master branch crates/config/src/lib.rs sets isolate: true. If the run is isolated, add four tests before deployment and confirm that each fails when its statement is removed: an unlock whose callback leaves a debt must revert with CurrencyNotSettled (src/PoolManager.sol:112); under the noIsolate modifier a take after an unlock returned must revert with ManagerLocked (113); two settles after one sync and one payment, with no take between them, must credit once (361); settleFor and clear must revert while locked (305, 310).
leads.why: The verifier confirmed that no test fails when line 112 is removed and that lines 113 and 361 are pinned only in a run that is not isolated, which neither the CI nor a current default forge test is. Each of the three statements guards all funds: without 112 a take needs no payment, without 113 any call after an unlock in the same transaction takes without an end check, without 361 one payment is credited twice. Two readers found all three in the text. A test is the only check in this repository that survives a later edit or a compiler setting change.

leads.question: When Celo schedules Karst, which predeploy implementations do its upgrade transactions install, and does the sixteen shape sweep from a stub at the PoolManager address give a different class for any of the 256 predeploy addresses or for 0xfd on the first day after activation?
leads.why: The L2 Contract Manager replaces predeploy code at the fork block. The sweeps of cycles 2 and 6 describe the code that is there now. A new fallback, a new payable function or a changed fee vault route at one of these addresses changes what a take or a currency call from the PoolManager does. The scripts stub_sweep.py and stub_single.py in the work directory of this unit rerun the test in three minutes.

leads.question: What does the planned migration of Celo to the second custom gas token design (celo-monorepo issue 11750, CgtV2UpgradeGroup in the client) do with the CELO token proxy and the transfer precompile, who would be authorised minters of LiquidityController, and does LiquidityController.mint deliver value to a recipient that has no receive function, such as the PoolManager?
leads.why: Celo is the only chain of the 21 where an ERC-20 address moves the native balance through a precompile that trusts one caller. A migration that changes the trusted caller, adds a second contract that can move native balances, or lets a minter push native value into the PoolManager between another account's sync and settle would reopen assumptions A2 and A3, which were cleared for the current design only. No specification of the Celo migration was found.

leads.question: Does OKX state anywhere whether the mainnet sequencer of X Layer starts xlayer-reth with the risk control filter enabled, and which rule categories the risk control service delivers?
leads.why: The chain data route is closed: the limit that does not depend on rules needs more than 10,000 internal native transfers in one transaction, and no such transaction was mined or is likely to be sent. F-024 can be settled only by an operator statement or by a test transaction that someone is willing to pay about 91,000,000 gas for, which this review does not send.

leads.question: Which target and selector pairs does the X Layer gasless whitelist at 0x19787404b0c70021b4752028f7e3a92313885B27 hold, and does any of them reach the PoolManager indirectly, for example a router or an aggregator that calls unlock on behalf of the sender?

The contract has more than two hundred storage branches and the public endpoints limit log queries to 100 blocks, so the entries were not listed.

leads.question: How much USDT, BUSD and other reward tokens have the 13 dividend trackers of BNB Smart Chain paid to the PoolManager, which public function starts a payout for a named account (process, processAccount, claim), and can a caller place that call between sync and settle of the reward token? leads.question: Run the full balance transfer test and the own transfer test on the 2,479,693 Base currencies of the two large code size groups (10,143 and 12,791 bytes) and on the two large hash families (7,865,260 and 2,680,543 members), ordered by the value of the paired balance. leads.question: List every pooled vault or receipt token on all 21 networks that has a conversion, migration or claim function taking the holder as an argument (claimFor, migrateFor, redeemFor, exitFor, convertFor, withdrawTo with an owner argument) and call each for the PoolManager by eth_call. attempts.answer: Every selector of 7,835 priced currencies above 1 USD that cycle 6 had not covered was called with the PoolManager as argument (636,744 trials), and 5,477 currencies of the full lists with a holder argument function name were tried (9,855 trials). ibBUSD on BNB Smart Chain stays the only token whose pooled balance a stranger can lower. leads.question: For WHITE on Ethereum and ARGUS on Arc: can the caller of take get the amount back out of the listed pair (skim on a v2 style pair, or a swap), so that a loop of take and settle drains the PoolManager balance at the cost of gas only? leads.why: On these networks fee collection was recognised from protocolFeesAccrued and balance moves from block balances. A trace would show the caller and the calls between sync and settle.

leads.question: Which pooled tokens charge the sender on top of the amount when the recipient is a listed pair, and for which of them does a transfer from that pair to the PoolManager arrive in full? Test every priced currency of every network against its v2 style pairs with the sequence transfer from the PoolManager to the pair, skim to the PoolManager, and compare the balance before and after.

The same test on 361 priced BNB Smart Chain currencies found no second case, and the other networks are untested.

attempts.answer: Tested on all 21 networks for 13,001 priced currencies with 128,687 recipient trials. WHITE on Ethereum (10 percent, v2 pair and v3 pool, full return through skim on the v2 pair) and ARGUS on Arc (1 percent, v3 pool, return arrives at 99 percent) are the only priced currencies that charge the sender above rounding. ARGUS is worth about 107,300 USD at the PoolManager. The seller that routes through take gains the charge, and the liquidity providers lose it.

leads.question: Which results of this and earlier cycles rest on eth_getLogs through bsc.api.pocket.network for blocks older than a few days? attempts.answer: Applied as a method rule: this unit made no log query on BNB Smart Chain and checked each of its two log counts against a second endpoint or against a balance. The earlier results that the lead names, the sNVB rebase history and the 393 rows of cycle 5, were not repeated here.

Done for the sNVB history, not done for the 393 rows of cycle 5 and the Initialize census of 78,255 currencies. The fault of the endpoint was reproduced on 2026-11-23: eth_getLogs through bsc.api.pocket.network for sNVB transfers out of the PoolManager in blocks 50,230,000 to 50,239,999 returned an empty list without an error, and so did a request for 500 blocks, while archive balances show two outflows at blocks 50,236,945 and 50,236,952 and the NodeReal endpoint returns 13 logs for the same 10,000 blocks. The whole sNVB history was then read from NodeReal in ranges of 50,000 blocks, with 33 failed requests repeated until none was left: 1,814 transfers out of the PoolManager, 973 transfers in and 8,942 rebase logs. Two checks that do not rest on the same logs agree with it. The rebase logs carry epochs 561 to 9,502 without a gap or a duplicate, and epoch() of the staking contract 0x6bcd1273eba684ff62614e41eff87123113112d1 reports 9,503 as the current number. For each of 40 intervals between 41 archive blocks, the change of balanceOf(PoolManager) divided by index() equals the sum of the logged transfers divided by the index at their time, to one part in a million. Result: the sNVB rebase on the PoolManager balance was paid out. 469 transactions between blocks 106,450,859 and 111,270,063 hold a rebase log and a transfer from the PoolManager and no transfer to it, 468 of them to the contract 0x3c69c0620ca6bd0df44c0aa8c39602f7c3ebdf27, for 94.0989 sNVB in total. Cycle 6 had recorded that sNVB was not scanned over its history. This is filed as an addition to F-091.

leads.question: List every pooled currency whose Transfer logs are emitted by a second contract (0x6369c3dadfc00054a42ba8b2c09c48131dd4aa38 with 0x1f426c51f0ef7655a6f4c3eb58017d2f1c381bff and the two EURe addresses on Ethereum, tokens with balance trackers on Robinhood Chain and BNB Smart Chain) and reconcile their census rows under the pooled address. A second address with a working transfer is one balance under two ids on Ethereum.

leads.question: What is the unverified hook 0xc81fd894c0ace037d133af4886550ac8133568e8 (6,024 bytes, flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeDonate, beforeSwapReturnDelta), who can register a pool on it (error 0x55e83950 in beforeInitialize), and whose are the 550.25 WETH on Ethereum and 2.70 cbBTC on Base it holds?

Read claim balances from a full ERC-6909 Transfer index and rerun the ranking.

The router is an ERC-6909 operator for all claims of the hook (14,720 USDC and 0.4 WETH at the PoolManager). The per pool reserve is the only bound in the verified code, so the settler decides whether a swapper can take a pool's reserve for a small input.

leads.why: rpc.monad.xyz, rpc2, rpc3 and the monadinfra endpoint answer Invalid params to a block override and have no eth_simulateV1, so 34 tokens worth 35 million USD were tested at the current time only, and 12 of them (AUSD, mUSD and ten wrapped stock tokens) without a caller balance.

leads.question: For every target token, call the functions with claim, reward, distribute, push, harvest, payout and dividend names with the PoolManager as argument and record all Transfer logs and native transfers to the PoolManager (eth_simulateV1 with traceTransfers where the endpoint has it), in place of the token's own balance.

A token that pays holder rewards in a second pooled asset to the PoolManager on a public call gives the caller a balance rise to book through sync and settle, as TITHE does in its own units (F-081). MONTRA on Elysium pays in KNTQ and excludes the PoolManager; others were not measured.

List role holders from RoleGranted and operator events of the tokens above 10,000 USD and test their public functions with the PoolManager as argument.

leads.question: Obtain verified source or decompile gAIX 0x0a4be7073bc336e451082502d768e8d644ca780c on Robinhood Chain (202,730 USD, 117 selectors without a name, words escrow and sweep), the MONTRA implementation 0x10b0292fb853966d3039d80bbef98b1a9507f55f on Elysium and the PAXG implementation 0xc623efe9cddf73e416a08d4cb81de738ba994037 on Base.
leads.why: Step 3 asks for a source reading and these have none at Sourcify or the reachable explorers, so their clearance rests on trials with fixed argument shapes.

leads.question: For every pooled currency with a balance, priced or not, run the stranger trial without a hand-out from the PoolManager at block times moved forward by 91, 400 and 1,500 days, with every state changing selector that takes an address or an address array, and record each call that lowers balanceOf(PoolManager).
leads.why: The idle rule search of this unit matched 20 function names. Imperium was found only because it exposes a lastActivity getter, and its acting function scanAndClean(address[]) is on no list. The full selector trials covered the 2,151 priced tokens only, and BankToken shows a period of 365 days that a 91 day shift finds only by the accident of its last transfer date. An unpriced token with real liquidity from third parties and a rule under another name is untested.

leads.question: Who provides liquidity in the pools of BankToken 0x718102f857b91eb573b78c41c654af2db05dd0b1 on Ethereum and of the DEAD copy 0x720f29e57cda0a987b7ff37ace02b7021aacbc0c on Polygon, and does any pool of an idle rule token hold funds of a party other than the token owner?
leads.why: Both Imperium pools turned out to be funded by the token owner alone, so the confirmed call harms nobody else today. The same reading was not done for the other two tokens, and the answer decides whether this class has a third party victim anywhere on the 21 networks beyond the Base case of F-085.

leads.question: Walk every finding of the five audit reports in docs/security/audits and of Known_Effects_of_Hook_Permissions.pdf against the text of src/. For each finding write one line with the hazard, the statement in src/ that closes it today with file and line, or the fact that nothing closes it, and the network features of ASSUMPTIONS.md A1 to A14 that the closing statement depends on. Start with the findings that name a property of a chain or of a token (OpenZeppelin C-01 and M-03, Trail of Bits 3 and 6, Certora M-01, I-01 and I-02, Spearbit 5.1.1 and 5.4.14) and then the 176 items of the ABDK draft. Use the prose of the reports as a list of hazards and stated fixes, and do not use code excerpts in them as a second copy to compare line by line.
leads.why: No unit has opened these files in six cycles. They are part of this repository and they are the only list of weaknesses known for this code. C-01 shows that the list contains a drain that exists on networks with a native ERC-20 face and on no other. Two guards that the reports describe (a lock check in sync and in collectProtocolFees) are absent from the source, and earlier units judged that without knowing the reports name them. A hazard that a report names and that the text does not close on one of the 21 networks would be an in-scope critical finding.

attempts.answer: Answered for the OpenZeppelin report, the Trail of Bits report and the hook permissions note. The other three reports belong to unit core-code-audit-walk-b. I read the two reports and the note page by page and wrote one result for each of the 24 OpenZeppelin findings, the 6 Trail of Bits findings, the 7 code quality items of its appendix C, its invariant tables and static invariants, and the 27 effects of the note. No finding of these documents is open in a way that lets an ordinary account take or lock funds of others. The fix that a report describes is absent from the source in two places: the lock guards of Trail of Bits finding 3 (sync and collectProtocolFees), and noDelegateCall on unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn from OpenZeppelin CR-01. Both are findings of this file with severity info. For the first I confirmed on the deployed contracts of Optimism, Polygon and Arc that a native fee collection runs inside an unlock while the native face is synced and that only the holder of that sync pays. OpenZeppelin C-01 is closed by src/PoolManager.sol:356 and 285-286, and a walk on all 21 deployed PoolManagers, with the real face on Celo, Arc, Polygon, Optimism and Zora, gave no double credit. OpenZeppelin M-03 and Trail of Bits finding 6 are unresolved by decision of the team and are recorded as low findings. The hook effects are by design and are tied to F-004. Everything on chain was tested against the contracts deployed today, because the checkout cannot be built in this session.

leads.question: On a machine that has solc 0.8.26, build this checkout with the settings of foundry.toml, set the immutable of NoDelegateCall to the override address, and run the three probes of core-code-test-pins.work and the 29 answer delegatecall test and the face walk of core-code-loose-guards.work against the built runtime bytecode placed by state override on the 21 RPC endpoints. Does every answer equal the one recorded for the deployed contract of that network, and do forge test and forge test --no-isolate both pass after the four tests of the verifier lead are added?
leads.why: Every on-chain behaviour test of six cycles ran on bytecode that nobody has shown to be a build of this checkout, and the tests of the repository pass without the end check of unlock, the lock close and the reset of the synced currency. Three readers found the statements in the text. A build that answers differently at one of them would let any account take without paying on every network. This merges the lead of core-code-test-pins, the lead of its verifier, L-016 and L-232 into one item.

leads.question: In the source of the Base client at the release that mainnet runs (the endpoint reports base/v1.5.6), list every code path of the B20 token precompile, the B20 factory 0xB20f000000000000000000000000000000000000 and the Policy Registry 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000002 that writes a balance or an allowance. For each path state who may call it, and answer three questions for a caller without a role: can it change balanceOf of another holder, can it make transfer return true while the amount is credited to an account other than the named recipient, and can it change whether the PoolManager passes a policy that a pooled token is bound to? Then run each such path by eth_call for OUSD 0xB2000000000000000000002fEb517dFeC7415344 with the PoolManager as the holder.
leads.why: L-119 and L-089 have waited since cycle 1 without an attempt. On Tempo the same reading of the TIP-20 precompile found a transfer that returns true while the amount goes to a guard (F-033). B20 is run by the chain for every token of the standard, so a path open to an ordinary account would reach every B20 pool at once, and the PoolManager held about 5.34 million OUSD when cycle 1 read it. The answer for Base was never taken from the client source.

attempts.answer: The client source at v1.5.6 was read for the stablecoin and asset logic v3, both dispatchers, the factory and the policy registry. Every balance write needs the owner as caller, an allowance from the owner, a token role, or the factory during creation of that same token. transfer credits the named recipient or reverts. Policy membership and policy admin change only on a call of the policy admin. Nineteen unprivileged calls against OUSD and the registry with the PoolManager as holder all reverted or returned zero at block 61,314,282. One issuer level fact is new and is filed under F-027: the block lists bound to OUSD and AMDc are each administered by one account without code.

leads.question: Extend the settlement model (cycles/002/core-code-invariants-settlement.model/settle_model.py or cycles/006/critic.work/face_model.py) with the four things all three models leave out and search to at least twelve steps: a second caller in the same transaction, collectProtocolFees for address(0) and for the face id as an action any caller can trigger with a fixed third party recipient, a hook that returns deltas in both currencies of a pool that names address(0) and the face, and a third id that mirrors the same balance and cannot pay out. Does any order end with all deltas at zero and one caller ahead, or with the PoolManager unable to pay a claim that another caller holds?
leads.why: The audit report in docs/security rates the native face case critical and names Celo and Polygon. The source closes the one caller case, and three models agree on that. The models never included the fee collection path, which has no lock check and exempts address(0) from the synced check (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52), or two callers that share a transaction. On Polygon and Arc a fee controller exists.

leads.question: Read the code of the seven fee controllers that core-code-loose-guards identified by selector list only (verified source where it exists, bytecode otherwise, and the 3,480 byte adapter on Arc first). Can any account call collect, can the caller choose the recipient, the currency or the amount, and can the call run inside the caller's own unlock? On Polygon and Arc, simulate a collection of address(0) while the native face is synced and state what the next settle of another payer in the same transaction returns.
leads.why: collectProtocolFees checks the caller and the synced token and never the lock (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The clearance that an open adapter moves accrued fees only to a fixed jar rests on the Ethereum source. An adapter that lets the caller name the recipient would hand accrued protocol fees to any account, and an open adapter on a network with a native face is the one input the settlement models never had.

leads.question: Run the sixteen shape sweep through a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address (stub_sweep.py under op-stack-custom-gas.work) on Ethereum, Monad and MegaETH against the precompiles, system contracts, predeploys, EntryPoints and wrapped native tokens of each. Add one shape that the sweep lacks: two reads of balanceOf(PoolManager) in one call with a storage clear, a value transfer and a transient write by the stub between them. Does any target answer the two reads with different words, or answer transfer with success while a balance of the stub changes?
leads.why: These three networks are the last ones with the four shape test only. The added shape looks for a ledger that moves inside one transaction without a payment, which is the only way a credit can arise at an address that is no token. Tempo has one such address (StorageCredits), found by reading and not by the sweep. MegaETH has an oracle and a timestamp service and Monad a staking precompile that were swept with single reads.

leads.question: For Dinari USD+ on Arbitrum One: decompile the implementation 0xff5bff8081eaee966bd74e9c0c059949df2345e1 and the public contract 0xb7541f225385104347539397a4e01abc1d4ea8bd. Which account signs the storage writes, does the signed message bind the chain id, the token address and a nonce, and which slots may a write name? Then find by code hash every other network of the 21 where the PoolManager holds a token that accepts selector 0x8078438b from the same kind of contract, and test whether a write signed for one network is accepted on another.
leads.why: The verifier found that the index of a token of which the PoolManager holds 1.07 million units moves through a signed write that any sender can submit, and that used writes revert on replay on Arbitrum One. A write that is valid on a second network, or one that an ordinary account can see before it lands, can be placed between that account's own sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 358-364). A write that may name any slot is an issuer power over balances that the finding does not yet describe. The behaviour was found on Arbitrum One, and no unit checked whether the PoolManagers of the other networks hold tokens that take writes the same way.

leads.question: Do the Robinhood stock tokens and USDG on Robinhood Chain have any path on which transfer returns true while the amount is credited to an account other than the named recipient, or held by a second contract, as TIP-20 does on Tempo for a recipient whose receive policy rejects the sender? Read the token implementation behind the proxies and send transfer(recipient, 1) from a stub at the PoolManager address to a restricted recipient, a paused share class and an unregistered recipient, reading both balances before and after.
leads.why: Lead L-214 asked this for three networks and was closed on the BNB Smart Chain part alone. A take that reports success and delivers nothing costs the withdrawing user the amount (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), which is finding F-033 on Tempo. Robinhood Chain has transfer rules enforced by the issuer and by the sequencer filter, and nobody ran the test there.

leads.question: Read WETH9() of the PositionManager and the wrapped native parameter of each Universal Router on these seven networks, as op-stack-custom-gas did for Celo. Which deployments name the native face itself, a contract that always reverts, or a token with other decimals than the native asset? For each, send the WRAP and UNWRAP actions and a native settle through the Quoter or by eth_call and state whether the call reverts, succeeds one to one, or succeeds with a different amount.
leads.why: On Celo the PositionManager and the first router name the CELO token, which is the native balance, as wrapped native, and on Arc they name a contract that reverts, as cycle 4 recorded. The other networks with a native asset other than ETH, or without one, were not read. Tempo has no native asset, HyperEVM and Elysium run a shorter PositionManager build of 19,965 bytes, and a wrapper with six decimals beside a native unit of eighteen would misprice every wrap. Most liquidity of ordinary users sits behind these contracts.

leads.question: For the 20 hooks per network that theme-hook-ledgers ranked by holdings: does the hook have any function that an ordinary account can call and that makes the hook call swap, modifyLiquidity or donate on the PoolManager with a PoolKey, amounts or hookData that the caller chooses? Read the source or the selector list and test by eth_call inside an unlock. Where the answer is yes, state what the skipped callbacks would have enforced and whose positions the hook address owns.
leads.why: The PoolManager skips every callback when msg.sender is the hook itself (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217, 253 and 293), and a position belongs to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161). A hook that forwards caller chosen calls therefore lets an ordinary account swap in its pools without the fee or the access rule that its callbacks apply, and act on liquidity that the hook owns for its users. No unit tried this lever. The probes of cycles 5 and 6 tested who may initialize a pool on a hook and which ledger the callbacks use.

leads.question: Read the four audit reports that arbitrum-family listed and did not open (Sequencer Feed Ticketing and Upgrade Action Contract, Yield Bearing Bridge, Tip Collection Toggler, OSP Soundness Guard) and the Stylus Permissioned Deployer report. Does the yield bearing bridge change the native balance or a bridged token balance of an account on the child chain without a transfer, is it deployed for Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain or Elysium, and does the tip toggler or the permissioned deployer change who may send a transaction or deploy code?
leads.why: The known weakness angle of the unit stopped at one of six reports. A bridge that pays yield by changing balances would touch assumption A2 for the native asset and for bridged tokens on a chain that adopts it, and Elysium already bridges its native asset from another chain.

leads.question: Elysium reports the client nitro/vlocal+unknown-unknown. Run the opcode and call pattern probes that the critic of cycle 1 used (TSTORE rollback in a reverted frame and in a reverted outer frame, TSTORE under STATICCALL, CALL with value to an account without code, return data of a failed call, the delegation probe of this cycle) in one eth_call each on Elysium and on Arbitrum One at the same ArbOS version, and compare the words. Does the Elysium team publish the commit it builds from?
leads.why: Every Elysium clearance assumes stock Nitro at v3.12.4. The network has 131,786 pools and 9,964 native units in the PoolManager, its node is a local build, and an upgrade that adds a predeploy and a precompile is announced. A difference in one probe word would show that the assumption fails before the upgrade arrives.

leads.question: On the first day after T14 activates on Tempo (2026-12-08): repeat the sixteen shape sweep and the inherited caller test, and answer one new question from the source at the activated commit. Can any party register or change a configuration of the ConfigurableAccount precompile for an address it does not control, and can a registered rule make a call reach the PoolManager with msg.sender equal to an account that holds ERC-6909 claims or positions without a signature of that account's root credential?
leads.why: The cycle 4 item read T14 from source before activation and covered the call shapes P1, P2, P3 and P5. Claims and positions are booked to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161, 301, 326 and 334, src/ERC6909.sol:25-48), so a new way to act as an account is a way to move its claims. F-051 already shows that a delegated credential with a token spending limit moves claims without limit.

leads.question: Which results of cycles 5 and 6 on BNB Smart Chain rest on eth_getLogs through bsc.api.pocket.network for blocks older than a few days? List them, repeat each through a second source, and add a count that does not depend on logs where one exists. On Base, confirm the Initialize census of 15,540,638 pools against the pool count of a second source for ten random windows.
leads.why: The verifier showed that the endpoint returned 191 of 323 logs without an error. A census that silently loses four logs in ten cannot support a statement that no row shows funds leaving without a debit.

leads.question: Repeat the Celo sweep of this cycle through a second endpoint and record web3_clientVersion beside every batch. Do the answers of the 319 addresses to the sixteen shapes differ between the reth build and the op-geth build that forno still serves, in particular for 0xfd, the CELO token and the four fee currency adapters?
leads.why: forno answered one of three version calls from a client that Celo no longer supports. The clearances for the native face on Celo cite probes through that endpoint, and the transfer precompile is implemented separately in each client.

leads.question: Does Nitro v3.12.4 contain the ArbOS 61 rules that Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain run under the unpublished build v3.13.0-rc.9, and has the source of that build or its consensus release been published since 2026-11-23? If it has, repeat the reading of parse_l2.go, tx_processor.go and the resolveCode change at that tag.
leads.why: All source readings of this cycle for the two chains were made at a release older than the one the nodes report. The transaction type walk and the filter analysis are only as good as the match between the two.

leads.question: Settle F-020 with one fact. Has any token other than USDC been activated for AQAv2 on HyperCore, and was its treasury address a contract or an address that had sent no transaction before? Read the spot deploy state from the info API and the first system transactions from each treasury address. If the HyperCore documentation or a validator release note states a check on the designated address, quote it.
leads.why: F-020 has been plausible since cycle 1 and leads L-065 and L-116 name this fact. If a designation needs proof of control, the PoolManager can never be named and the finding drops to info. If a contract address was accepted once, the operator hazard is confirmed.

leads.question: Settle F-024 with one fact: a statement by OKX, in documentation, release notes, a governance post or an answer to a direct question from the owner, on whether the mainnet sequencer of X Layer starts xlayer-reth with the risk control filter enabled. Chain data cannot show it, as this cycle established.
leads.why: F-024 has been plausible since cycle 1. The filter is in the mandatory release and switched off by default, and the only rule independent trace would need a transaction of about 69,000,000 gas that this review does not send.

leads.question: Settle F-062 with one fact: read the payload builder of the MegaETH sequencer in the public repositories of megaeth-labs for the order in which it takes candidates from the pool and for what it does with a candidate that the block limiter skipped. Does a skipped transaction keep its place ahead of newer arrivals in the next block?
leads.why: F-062 is plausible on an inference from block contents, and lead L-170 has one inconclusive attempt. Arrival order across blocks would make the delay a standing one for every user at a known price per day, and fee order would bound it at one block.

leads.question: In crates/evm and crates/precompiles of arc-node at the commit that mainnet runs: can native value reach an account without a call to it, through SELFDESTRUCT, a block reward, a fee refund, a system transfer or the Native Coin Authority, in an amount that is not a multiple of 10^12 wei? State the rule for each of the five.
leads.why: Three models agree that the only gain on Arc needs such an inflow while 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 is synced and that it stays below 10^12 wei per settle. This one fact closes the open point of two cycle 2 items and of the verifier lead of this cycle.

leads.question: Robinhood Chain answers eth_call and eth_estimateGas without applying its transaction filter. Is the same true on Soneium for the restricted list of F-030 and on X Layer for the builder filter of F-024: does a simulated call that touches a listed contract succeed on the public endpoint while the sequencer would leave the transaction out?
leads.why: Wallets and routers simulate before they send. Where simulation and inclusion disagree, a user of a pool that touches a listed address learns of the block only when the transaction fails or never lands. The behaviour was shown on Robinhood Chain in this cycle and was not tested on the two other networks with an operator list.

leads.question: X Layer gives zero priced transactions to listed target and selector pairs. List the pairs of the whitelist at 0x19787404b0c70021b4752028f7e3a92313885B27 from its storage or logs, and check for Tempo sponsored transactions and for Arc whether any public sponsor or paymaster pays for calls that reach the PoolManager through a router or an account abstraction entry point.
leads.why: Filling a boundary tick to the liquidity cap (F-038) and other griefing cost gas today. A free path into the PoolManager would remove that cost inside the budget of the sponsor. The X Layer whitelist has more than two hundred storage branches and only six targets were tried.

leads.question: OpenZeppelin M-03 is left to the periphery. Do the deployed PositionManagers (the 23,877 byte build on 19 networks and the 19,965 byte build on HyperEVM and Elysium) reject a mint or an increase when the pool price makes the amounts exceed the caller's maxima, and do the published SDK and the launch pad hooks with most pools pass maxima that bind?
leads.why: Core accepts any starting price from any account and moves the price of an empty pool for free (src/PoolManager.sol:117-134, src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437). If a widely used path adds first liquidity without a binding bound, an ordinary account can take part of that deposit on every network.

leads.question: Celo and Zora have an address that reports the PoolManager's native balance and no protocol fee controller. When the owner sets a controller there, is its collect function open to any account as on the eight networks that have one, and does a native fee collection then run while the face is synced?
leads.why: The synced currency check in collectProtocolFees skips address(0) (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49). On Optimism, Polygon and Arc that already lets a native collection lower the face balance between sync and settle. Celo is the one network where the face can also be paid out by take, so the walk should be repeated there once a controller exists.

leads.question: Which behaviour is the build for the 21 deployments meant to have: the lock check that src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 and the Trail of Bits fix review describe, or the synced currency check that src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52 and test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039 pin? If the lock check returns, which tests and which of the eight fee adapters change behaviour?
leads.why: The interface comment, the unused _isUnlocked hook and the audit record say one thing and the source and its tests say another. The ledger judged the present text harmless. A restored lock check would change what F-014 and F-071 describe and would make collection revert whenever it is triggered inside any unlock.

leads.question: For each of the 21 networks, can an ordinary account place one transaction directly before and one directly after a pending donate or fee distributing swap of another party, and which hook or distributor contracts that call donate hold an earlier accrued balance that any caller can make them pay out? Start with the Donate senders on Ethereum, Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Arbitrum One listed in cycles/007/core-code-audit-walk-b.work/raw/donate_logs.json.
leads.why: Spearbit 5.1.1 and Certora M-02 are open in the source by decision. The loss is real only where a donation is not funded by the call that triggers it, or where another party's donation can be bracketed. Four networks show donations today and this unit read only four transactions.

leads.question: In a build of this checkout with solc 0.8.26 and via_ir, does the generated code clean the bytes4 returned by ParseBytes.parseSelector before the comparison at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152 and the uint24 returned by parseFee before it is written to Pool.SwapParams at src/PoolManager.sol:209-215?
leads.why: These are the two places where the fix for Certora L-03 and ABDK CVF-44 rests on the compiler and not on a mask in the text. If the selector comparison used raw words, a correct hook would be rejected, which would show at once in tests, so the risk is low. It belongs with the open build leads L-483 and L-016.

leads.question: What did the change that Certora cites as the partial fix of I-01 (pull request 786) add, and is that statement still in src? The report gives the number and no description.
leads.why: It is the one fix among the three reports that this unit could not map to a line. If it was a guard that limits who may open deltas during an unlock, its absence would matter to integrators that make untrusted calls inside an unlock.

leads.question: BNB Smart Chain shows 22 Donate events of the PoolManager in blocks 135,322,108 to 135,327,108, 13 of them from 0x8c7852bb503b4579c28a6fa2bcf112c7657a6488, 4 from 0x15544eba1a7c7054a4bedceb876a7bf1a6ac258b and 2 from 0x02c3d34faad49df254b20724e62a36b6a09f6488. Does any of these donors, or any donor on the six other networks for which the audit walk has no log count (Base, World Chain, X Layer, Polygon, Avalanche, Monad), pay out a balance that was accrued before the call that triggers the donation, on a call open to any account?
leads.why: The donation capture finding rests at low because every donation read so far is funded by the transaction that triggers it. The unit's raw file has no count for seven networks, and BNB Smart Chain turns out to have donors. One donor with an earlier accrued balance and a public trigger would raise the rating to medium for that pool. Counts on BNB Smart Chain need a second source, since one endpoint was found to drop logs in an earlier cycle.

leads.question: Compute the SALT bucket ids of the fee growth slots of the 36 exposed positions (raw/mega_positions.pkl in the work directory lists pool, owner, ticks, salt and slot) with the hasher of the SALT repository, and read the capacity of those buckets from a block witness (mega_getBlockWitness) or a stateless validator. Is any bucket that holds a PoolManager slot above 256 today?
leads.why: The first finding rests on the specification and sources for the growth of a bucket. One grown bucket on mainnet would confirm the pricing on chain, and a grown bucket under a PoolManager slot would show that a position is already cut off from the L1 route.

leads.question: For every network with an L1 forced inclusion path: what is the largest gas limit one forced transaction may carry (simulate depositTransaction or the delayed inbox call with rising gas limits), and does a PositionManager removal fit with the storage prices of that network?
leads.why: The MegaETH portal carries a cap of 1,000,000 gas that its documentation does not mention and that earlier cycles replaced by the 20,000,000 per block figure. The same test costs one eth_call per network. In this cycle the OP Mainnet and Base portals accepted a deposit of 5,000,000 gas, and the other networks were not tested.

leads.question: Read the verified source of the MegaETH OptimismPortal implementation 0x55400445e384393f9c1be23e7e734e8d44ed9fd9 on Ethereum. Besides the 1,000,000 gas cap and the MEGA_SYSTEM_ADDRESS check, does it change the withdrawal path or the handling of deposits from contracts?
leads.why: The portal is the only exit and entry that does not depend on the sequencer, and its bytecode differs from the standard build in at least two places. Only strings in the bytecode were read.

leads.question: What does the MegaETH pool do with a transaction that was skipped for a block level limit: does it run ahead of transactions that arrived later, and is there a limit on queued state growth per sender? Ask the operator, or look for a block whose later mini-blocks are empty after a transaction with about 1,000 new entries and read the first mini-block of the next block.
leads.why: This is the one open link of F-062. The public gateway exposes no pending transactions, so the answer cannot come from a passive capture.

leads.question: After mainnet moves to v0.16.6 or later, repeat the swap differential of cycle 4 on the deployed PoolManager. The release changes how the compiler emits shifts by a literal value and CLZ.
leads.why: TickMath, SqrtPriceMath and the packed types shift by literal amounts throughout. The cycle 4 comparison ran on the build before this change.

leads.question: Which function lets a depositor of the vault contracts 0x5f16b71cc05b146d73e181354b1c8ac89fc4bbc3 and 0xdc41ab847d922fe4375d7d050f518480634ff0e9 (same 20,944 byte code, 21 live positions in the MegaETH PoolManager) withdraw, and does eth_estimateGas for that call from a real depositor stay under 1,000,000 gas with calldata under 2,225 bytes?
leads.why: A cleared item of this cycle says a removal fits in a forced transaction when no bucket has grown. That was measured for the PositionManager only. Every call that removed liquidity of 0xdc41ab847d922fe4375d7d050f518480634ff0e9 used 1.17 to 3.24 million gas. If the withdrawal call is of the same size, depositors of these vaults have no L1 exit today and the 12 hour bound of F-017 does not apply to them. The actor would be operator, since the sequencer route works.

leads.question: The MegaETH portal requires a gas limit of at least 21,000 plus 440 per calldata byte and at most 1,000,000, so a forced call carries at most 2,225 bytes of calldata. Which exits need more: a PositionManager call that closes several positions, a call through a Safe or another smart account that owns a position, a Universal Router path, a claim burn through a wrapper?
leads.why: The cap on calldata follows from two portal checks that the documentation does not state, and earlier cycles assumed a forced budget of 20,000,000 gas. An owner whose only way to act is a long call has no forced route. This also needs the sequencer to refuse the owner.

leads.question: evm/execution.rs lines 883 to 918 at tag v1.7.3 add new account storage gas of 25,000 times (multiplier minus 1) to the intrinsic gas of a deposit whose sender account is empty. Can any account grow the SALT bucket of a chosen address so that every forced transaction from that address fails the intrinsic gas test at the 1,000,000 cap, and do holders of positions or claims exist whose MegaETH account is empty (received by transfer, never funded)?
leads.why: At multiplier 64 the charge is 1,575,000 gas. This would close the forced route for a whole sender, where the first finding closes it for one position. It reaches only accounts with nonce zero, no balance and no code, and again needs the sequencer to refuse the owner.

leads.question: Which HyperCore record names an AQAv2 treasury address? Read the explorer block details for HyperCore blocks between 1,020,511,746 (the authorizeAqav2Role action of 2026-06-02) and the first treasury system transaction on 2026-06-12 03:59 UTC, and look for a validator vote or deployer action that contains 0xc20699185c15D0a2fD65779BB5d69f5b0B113c00. Find Circle's technical deployer account and read its actions as well.
leads.why: F-020 stays plausible on this one fact. The deployer's documented action has no address field, so the record is a validator vote or an undocumented action. Its form shows who can name an address and whether a change needs a new vote.

leads.question: Find or wait for a RawAction log from an emitter other than CoreWriter whose named user holds a HyperCore balance and whose payload is a valid action, and read that user's HyperCore ledger. A search of the whole history for the topic 0x8c7f585fb295f7eb1e6aeb8fba61b23a4fe60beda405f0045073b185c74412e3 needs about five million logs to be read, and this cycle covered the last 600,000 blocks.
leads.why: The node's emitter test is shown on chain for the bridge log and only inferred for CoreWriter. Any contract can forge the log, so the inference is strong, and a direct case would close the inherited caller question for CoreWriter with primary evidence.

leads.question: Read the implementation behind the nine strategy token proxies (for example 0x8593b70c65798282a0a86a02f9770fb8ad1a6f70, the one pool with three swaps) and state when transfer from the PoolManager is allowed. Can a buyer in these pools receive the token through the deployed routers, and does the hook's use of address(poolManager).balance to choose between a take and a claim mint matter for the native side?
leads.why: The tokens refuse a plain transfer from the PoolManager with InvalidTransfer(). They belong in the token list of the transfer side effects theme and in the table behind F-083. The hazard is limited to the product's own pools.

leads.question: Lead L-415 cannot be answered from HyperEVM history: no transaction that emitted a PoolManager log ever left a token sync behind. A transaction that calls sync alone emits no log, so search the callers of the PoolManager by tracing whole blocks around native settles on an indexer that stores call traces, or accept the in-execution probes of the official node as the evidence for A1.
leads.why: The block producing node is closed. The probes of this cycle show its behaviour inside one execution and the archive client reproduces every block, and the boundary between two transactions of one block is still shown only by the archive client.

leads.question: Which record tells HyperCore the ERC-20 address that AQAv2 system transactions call? For USDC the linked contract in spotMeta is the CoreDepositWallet 0x6b9e773128f453f5c2c60935ee2de2cbc5390a24, an upgradeable proxy, while the unsigned transfers go to the token 0xb88339cb7199b77e23db6e890353e22632ba630f. Read the CoreDepositWallet implementation for a token getter and ask the Hyperliquid team whether the node reads it at run time or stores the address at the vote.
leads.why: F-020 depends on two records, the treasury address and the token that is moved out of it. If the node reads the token address from the linked contract, the party that can upgrade that contract chooses which token leaves a recorded treasury address without a new vote. This changes who the privileged actor of F-020 is and does not open a path for an ordinary account.

leads.question: For every currency of an initialized pool on the seven chains (the complete lists of cycle 6), what does a transfer of 1 unit from the PoolManager to a fresh address cost in gas, which tokens need more than 1,000,000 gas, and for which of those does the cost grow with a number that any account can raise (holders, checkpoints, registered recipients)?
leads.why: MUPPETS on World Chain shows the pattern: 4.55 million gas per transfer today, 14,143 more per holder, and no transfer possible above about 1,210 holders because of the 16,777,216 gas cap. That token is in no pool. A pooled token of the same kind would let any account freeze takes of it for a few dollars of gas, and the tests of earlier cycles compared balances and storage and never recorded gas.

leads.question: Lead L-352 carried forward: after Lagoon activates on OP Sepolia and Unichain Sepolia (target 10 December 2026), which implementations sit behind 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000022 to 0x28 and 0x30, and what does each return to the sixteen call shapes through a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address?
leads.why: The slots are empty on all four networks today, so the cycle 5 clearance still rests on source that is not deployed.

leads.question: Which op-reth revision do the OP Mainnet sequencer, World Chain v2.8.2 and the Conduit build of Zora (conduit-op-reth v2.5.1) run, and does each contain optimism pull request 22778 (bare RLP deposits rejected) and reth pull request 28264 (trie iterator fix)?
leads.why: Both fixes were tied to release numbers only. A chain without the first fix leaves its batcher able to place an unsigned deposit with a chosen sender, and a chain without the second can stall or serve wrong proofs.

leads.question: What does the unverified contract 0xd7c91ecad10a33bf6f77f8c24089cad37be7a9f9 do with the two counters that every BB transfer raises, and does it hold a limit per period or a threshold at which transfers of BB 0x4c447f3b26fa2c9d782eeb4d9dd47c7a2d2a52b8 start to revert?
leads.why: The PoolManager holds 99 percent of the BB supply. Sixty round trips passed, which excludes only a cap below 120 balances. A volume limit above that would let any account stop takes of BB with repaid takes.

leads.question: Why does PIZZA 0xa1f70fbc0ccb017f0c2e10cd4581c543082fcdcc refuse a transfer from a fresh address that has just received the full amount from the PoolManager, and can a third party put the PoolManager into the same state by sending it a small amount?
leads.why: If the refusal is a waiting time that starts on receipt, any account could block takes of the token by repeated dust transfers to the PoolManager. The PoolManager holds 170 PIZZA.

leads.question: Rerun the round trip state diff for the 233 World Chain tokens that failed on the two requests per second limit and for the 18 Soneium tokens that were not reached.
leads.why: The clearance of lead L-306 covers 457 of 690 tokens on World Chain and 70 of 88 on Soneium.

leads.question: Simulate the two party AGL sequence on OP Mainnet or Base: a buy that ends with mint, then a sell by a second caller in the same transaction. Does the second payment revert with ForaDaCota as the hook source implies?
leads.why: The finding of this cycle that extends F-074 rests on the hook source alone.

leads.question: Does the Base release v1.5.6 that the endpoint reports contain merge commit 5c7850b02e103645022e1374ea854aab4e5879f1 of base/base pull request 4972, which rejects a deposit body without the 0x7e type byte?
leads.why: The cleared item on bare RLP deposits left the Base client unconfirmed. The pull request is merged, and only the link from the merge to the running release is missing. Without the fix the party that signs batches could place an unsigned deposit with a chosen sender.

leads.question: After 24 November 2026 15:00 UTC on Moderato and after 8 December 2026 15:00 UTC on mainnet, register one configurable account (or find one) and repeat the 15 shape sweep on it and on 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 with the PoolManager address as caller. Does a registered account return success with empty data for empty calldata and revert for transfer, balanceOf, unlockCallback and the hook selectors, as shim.rs at commit 697ea97 says?
leads.why: The precompile part was confirmed with a simulated block time. The registered account part is read from source only, because registration sits in an account extension that a state override cannot set. A registered account that answered transfer with success and empty data would behave like a currency without code that also holds state.

leads.question: Obtain the source or a decompilation of the bridged WETH implementation 0xdc0518fa6940ecc05dbe5988a93c5a6e43fec52e on Arc and name the storage slot 0x3dd25e0047d6d00b4d8443336d6cde00c8d01c381664a6499f183b835193c160 that every transfer reads, and the 13 selectors I could not match to a name (01ca4d43, 06923592, 06bfcec6, 40ed6916, 5c49b8c0, 5e4b599a, 604cfaaa, 77e7370f, 7f3f4fde, 84df9f72, c3cfb506, e34e32c0, f47b1eb9). The slot holds zero today and is read whatever the sender and recipient are, which fits a global switch. This concerns issuer powers and would extend the blocklist finding of this cycle.

leads.question: Do other tokens issued through the CrossChainTokenService 0x431871229103b780868f8C6BB820cd16ECf942BC on Arc use the same adapter 0x3ebe1f103151890346cd7dbcec1c596cc50ef58e, and does the PoolManager hold any of them?

leads.why: The borrowed call input and the absence of nested transactions are properties of one revision of an interpreter that changes every few weeks.

leads.question: Who can upgrade the CrossChainTokenService proxy 0x431871229103b780868f8C6BB820cd16ECf942BC on Arc or rewrite its slot 0x86a0e84c7d929f61fb2e716e558792f9ee8d701914df21037b29796118dd8e02, which holds the denylist adapter address that every transfer of the bridged WETH token 0x128cC466B61f542da60c70e3aA11c10e19B84EDB consults, and can the 597 byte adapter 0x3ebe1f103151890346cd7dbcec1c596cc50ef58e be replaced?

leads.question: Run the charged transfer test of this unit on the unpriced currencies with the most Transfer logs at the PoolManager, starting with token T 0x4ef42e4cf51cd779e9947db65b629ecd8c92b1da on BNB Smart Chain and with every pooled token that answers mainPool(), pair() or uniswapV2Pair() with an address that has code.

leads.question: Do the deployed Universal Router versions and the common aggregators pass a v2 pair or v3 pool as the recipient of take when a route goes from a v4 pool into a v2 or v3 pool, and how much ARGUS and WHITE volume takes that path per day?
leads.why: When routers do this on their own, ordinary swaps charge the PoolManager without any intent, and the rate of the ARGUS shortfall follows from routed volume. 1,297 charge transfers exist on Arc and 766 on Ethereum.

leads.question: List the tokens created by the ARGUS portal 0x0f1c7cb26d6cd36bd4189e41947658b39437587a and its implementation 0x122c82cfca7a3a2227285cc21f4522e8f551db3a, and test each one that has a v4 pool for the 1 percent sender charge on a transfer to its mainPool().

leads.question: Build selector files for the full currency lists of Robinhood Chain, World Chain and MegaETH and run the holder argument trial by function name on them.
leads.why: The full list trial ran on 17 networks. On these three only the priced currencies were tried, 491 on Robinhood Chain, 89 on World Chain and 11 on MegaETH.

leads.question: Which pooled tokens can be burned or converted for a holder through a separate migrator, staking or vault contract that is not the token or its implementation?
leads.why: The trials call the token and its implementation only. A migrator with migrateFor(holder) that holds a burn role on the old token would not be seen.

leads.question: Does one unlock with a one sided liquidity add on the ARGUS main pool 0x6a3bacaa6493734c1ac221ebf42cf530a96c1e02 paid by take inside the mint callback, followed by burn and collect to the PoolManager, cost the caller only the 1 percent buy charge, and how much of both charges reaches the creator wallet 0x7d613c6316ede9d257f3bf512777cb4ea4a6bee4 after swapBack and dispatch?
leads.why: config() shows that 100 percent of the ARGUS charge goes to the creator wallet after a bounty of 0.5 percent and a protocol fee of 1 percent. If the round costs 1 percent, the creator gains about 1 percent of the amount per round out of 46.6 million pooled ARGUS (about 106,000 USD), and any other account can remove the same share at a cost equal to the damage. The finding states 3 percent. The route was derived from source and not simulated.

leads.question: Which other portals and implementation versions of the launchpad behind ARGUS exist on Arc, which of their tokens does the PoolManager hold, and does any of them have a dividend tracker (dividendBps above 0)?
leads.why: The tracker interface in the verified ARGUS source pays native USDC to every holder, lets any account call reclaimStranded for a contract holder that cannot receive native value, and credits deposits to whoever holds at the moment dispatch runs, which any account can call. A pooled token of that kind would let a caller borrow the pooled balance through take for one transaction and collect the dividend share of the PoolManager. ARGUS and BBASRUS both have no tracker. The portal check covered one portal.

leads.question: Rerun the charged transfer test with the price list taken from DexScreener in addition to DefiLlama, and for each hit test whether a sender that holds exactly the amount is refused or pays no charge.
leads.why: Token T on BNB Smart Chain charges 3 percent on top and has a DexScreener price while DefiLlama has none, so the sweep counted it as unpriced. The exact balance test separates tokens like WHITE, where the route through take saves the seller the charge, from tokens like ARGUS, where the charge is clamped and the seller gains nothing.

leads.question: On the first day after Jenner activates on BNB Smart Chain (2026-12-08 02:30 UTC), run one visit that answers L-346, L-418, L-042, L-406 and the Jenner lead of core-code-loose-guards together. For one live CAS20 token, or for the CAS20 address range and 0x70 if token creation is still closed: (a) the sixteen call shapes through a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, (b) transfer, transferFrom, approve and balanceOf with DELEGATECALL, CALLCODE and STATICCALL from a contract that the stub called, with and without value in that frame, (c) sync, a transfer in, settle and take through the deployed PoolManager, including a transfer from the PoolManager to itself and a transfer of zero, (d) every function of core/vm/cas20.go at the activated commit that writes a balance, with who may call it. Does any call by an account without a role change balanceOf(PoolManager), or return success for a transfer that moves nothing or moves more than the amount?
leads.why: The sweeps of this network describe addresses that answer like accounts without code until the fork, and the token logic was read on a testnet and on the master branch. CAS20 is token code inside the node on one of the two networks with the most swaps. A token that acts on an inherited caller, or whose balance at the PoolManager a stranger can raise between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364), would let an ordinary account take pooled funds as soon as a pool holds one.

leads.question: Run the inherited caller test of cycle 7 where it has not run on chain. Place a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address and a second stub as its callee by state override, and from the callee use DELEGATECALL, CALLCODE and STATICCALL as well as CALL, once without value and once in a frame that received value as the recipient of a native take. Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium: every ArbOS precompile from 0x64 to 0x74, 0xff and 0xa4b05 with one view and one state changing selector each, on the builds that run today. Arc: Memo and the addresses 0x1800...02 to 0x1800...07 (the critic runs of this cycle cover 0x1800...00, 0x1800...01 and Multicall3From). Does any call act with the PoolManager as the account, send a message in its name, or accept a stated value that no balance backs?
leads.why: The PoolManager hands control to caller chosen code with itself as msg.sender in the unlock callback, in every hook call and in every native payout (src/PoolManager.sol:110, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, src/types/Currency.sol:48). The angle ran on Monad, MegaETH and HyperEVM in cycle 7, on Base and Tempo tokens in cycle 6, and on two Arc precompiles in the critic checks. For the Nitro chains the rejection rests on precompiles/precompile.go lines 754 to 757 at v3.12.4, while Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain run the unpublished build v3.13.0-rc.9 and Elysium a local build. The ArbOS precompiles hold no token balances, so the likely worst case is a message or withdrawal that names the PoolManager as sender.

leads.question: For each network whose block producer is closed source or reports no version (HyperEVM, MegaETH, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, OP Mainnet), find one mined transaction in which a call frame that had entered PoolManager.unlock reverted and a later frame of the same transaction completed an unlock, for example an on-chain quote by revert followed by the swap. Read it with debug_traceTransaction where an endpoint serves it, or from the receipt together with a replay of the failed inner call. Does such a transaction exist on each of the five, and did the later unlock succeed?
leads.why: The rollback of transient writes with a reverted frame is shown on these networks by RPC nodes and third party clients. A mined transaction of this shape is evidence from the node that produced the block: had the unlock flag survived the reverted frame, the later unlock would have reverted with AlreadyUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:105, src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27). A producer that keeps transient writes of a reverted frame would let a caller keep a settle credit whose payment was rolled back (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41). The expected answer is that all five behave as Ethereum does, and the test replaces an assumption with an observation.

attempts.answer: Robinhood Chain: yes. Transaction 0x222fe1797dd7dcfd16c424c6d6abc0fd48c589c5194ea44ad7184fc932a73e10 has an unlock that reverted after its callback swapped, followed by an unlock that succeeded, so the producer rolled back the transient unlock flag. Elysium: not answerable, because its trace method needs an API key. HyperEVM, MegaETH and OP Mainnet belong to other units.

Answered yes for HyperEVM (3 transactions) and MegaETH (8,481 in this cycle, 1,333 in cycle 10), each with the later unlock completed and the receipt equal to re-execution. Robinhood Chain, Elysium and OP Mainnet were outside this unit.

leads.question: Finish the delegated account test on the natively implemented addresses that cycles 6 and 7 did not cover: give an account an EIP-7702 designator that points at each HyperEVM read precompile 0x0800 to 0x0814, at each ArbOS precompile, and at the Arc precompiles 0x1800...00 to 0x1800...07, by state override, and call that account from the PoolManager address with transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address), empty calldata with value and one hook selector. Does the node run the native logic, and if so under which address and which caller?
leads.why: Cycle 6 ran this for tokens on Base, Tempo, Arc, Celo and the Chapel testnet, and cycle 7 for Monad and MegaETH, with four different answers (undefined opcode, empty success, a revert of the proxy, a failed call). A node that ran native logic for a delegated account would give an ordinary account a second address for one piece of chain state. The face walks show that a second address for one balance gives no gain by itself, so the expected result is a clearance.

leads.question: For the ten most used hooks of each of these networks (start with ZoraV4CoinHook 0xc8d077444625eb300a427a6dfb2b1dbf9b159040, ContentCoinHook 0x9ea932730a7787000042e34390b8e435dd839040 and ClankerHookStaticFeeV2 0xb429d62f8f3bffb98cdb9569533ea23bf0ba28cc on Base, 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium and 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc on Monad): does the code contain TSTORE, which transient slots does a swap write, are they indexed by pool id, and are they reset before the call returns? For each hook that leaves a value, simulate two swaps in one transaction, the first through a pool that the caller created with the same hook and the second through a pool with other users' liquidity, and compare the second result with the same swap alone. Then repeat with the second swap started from inside the first one, through a token of the caller's pool that calls back when the hook or the PoolManager moves it.
leads.why: AGL shows a hook whose transient quota survives the unlock and changes the outcome of the next call. initialize accepts any pool that names an existing hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), so the caller controls one of the two pools. If a hook with return delta flags reads an amount or a fee from a transient slot that another pool wrote, the caller can move the delta that the PoolManager books to the second pool's swapper or to the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:285-315). The loss would fall on users of a pool whose hook the attacker did not write.

attempts.answer: Not done: the owner set this cycle on opcodes and ruled out hook sweeps; the Arc part of the lead stays open for a hook unit.

leads.question: Which Ethereum fork is active and which is scheduled on mainnet on the day of the visit (eth_config on an endpoint that serves it, the fork list of the execution specifications, the meta EIP of the next fork)? Does the scheduled fork add a transaction type whose parts run with different senders or roles, and does its specification say whether transient storage is cleared between those parts? Run the sixteen shape sweep through a forwarding stub on Ethereum, which is the reference for every other sweep.

leads.question: At commit 697ea97 of tempoxyz/tempo, which system transactions does the block executor accept: with which sender, which targets and which input, and what does it do with a transaction whose sender is the zero address and whose target is an ordinary contract? Can a type 0x76 transaction, a fee payer signature or a keychain signature recover to the zero address?
leads.why: protocolFeeController is the zero address on Tempo, and setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees test msg.sender against that value and nothing else (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48). An account that could call as the zero address could set the protocol fee to 1,000 pips per direction on every pool and withdraw what accrues. If only a block proposer can place such a transaction the actor is operator.

leads.question: F-062, the one fact: when the MegaETH sequencer skips a transaction because the block has reached 1,000 new state entries, does that transaction run ahead of transactions that arrived later, and is there a limit on queued state growth per sender? Look for a block whose later mini-blocks are empty after a transaction with close to 1,000 new entries and read the first mini-block of the next block, or ask the operator. This merges L-170, L-176, L-177 and the new lead of high-throughput.
leads.why: The finding is plausible for the fourth cycle on this fact. If skipped transactions keep their place, a paid queue delays every later transaction by its length, which together with the forced route cap of this cycle would be a paid delay of exits by an ordinary account. If they do not, the finding is refuted.

leads.question: F-020, the one fact: which HyperCore record names an AQAv2 treasury address and the token that is moved out of it (a validator vote, an undocumented deployer action, or a getter of the linked CoreDepositWallet 0x6b9e773128f453f5c2c60935ee2de2cbc5390a24 read at run time), and does the node accept an address with code in that role? Read the explorer block details between HyperCore block 1,020,511,746 and the first treasury system transaction on 2026-06-12 for an entry that contains 0xc20699185c15D0a2fD65779BB5d69f5b0B113c00. This merges L-065, L-116, L-276, L-323, L-422 and the two new leads of this cycle.
leads.why: The finding has been plausible since cycle 1. The answer decides who the privileged actor is (the validator set, a deployer, or whoever can upgrade the linked contract). It does not open a path for an ordinary account.

leads.question: F-024, the one fact: is the risk control filter of the X Layer block builder switched on for the mainnet sequencer? Take the observation that lead L-263 names. Also answer the X Layer and Soneium parts of L-321 that no unit attempted: by which rule does an address enter the X Layer TxBlacklist and the Soneium restricted list, and can an ordinary account cause an entry for the PoolManager or for a pooled token?
leads.why: F-024 has been plausible since cycle 1 on this flag, and the family did not run in cycle 7.
